name: Jaku / Labɨr
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger & Timothy Terna. 2024. An introduction to Jaku [jku], a barely documented Jarawan Bantu language of Central Nigeria. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation, working document (Jos, 18 September 2024). of the Academia.edu pagehttps://www.academia.edu/123970682/AN_INTRODUCTION_TO_JAKU_jku_A_BARELY_DOCUMENTED_JARAWAN_BANTU_LANGUAGE_OF_CENTRAL_NIGERIA(PDF itself login-gated).
catalog_locator: Section 2.2 'Vowels' and 2.3 'Tone', p. 4 of the main text, chars ~79,925-80,700
catalog_quote: There is no evidence for either contrastive length or nasalisation in Jaku. Long vowels are marked as heard in the dictionary dataset, but these need to be reconfirmed with speakers before claiming a phonemic status for them. As noted above, it is possible this is variation in younger speakers. 2.3 Tone Jaku has three level tones and apparently no glide tones. Rising tones are heard in some numerals (Table 14) but not systematically in the lexicon. These are examples of minimal triplets; bál to count bāl liver bàl large river tán bow tān to learn tàn to plait yál to prevent yāl to jump yàl to fly Examples of homophones; yál smoke, jump fúr go out, locust beans yíl goat, to follow, to give birth
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only modern description treats Jaku/Labɨr as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L; the 2026 follow-up adds rising and falling contours); neither it nor any other located source says anything about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes only: rising tones in some numerals; future marked by a falling tone on the subject pronoun; perfective and remote past involve stem tone changes.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on monosyllabic and polysyllabic citation forms; no prosodic-word or phrase-level prominence discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench & Terna 2024 and Blench 2026 describe Labɨr (autonym láɓɨ́r; exonym Jaku/ʤàkú), ISO jku = Glottolog labi1245, spoken in Alkaleri and Bauchi LGAs, Bauchi State; data elicited from a speaker working group in Jos, 2024. This is exactly the target languoid, not a neighbouring Jarawan variety. (C. R. Green's published Jarawan phonology is on Mbat, a Jar-cluster lect, and does not bear on Jaku.)

Read the whole of Sec. 2 Phonology (2.1 Consonants p.3, 2.2 Vowels p.4, 2.3 Tone p.4), Sec. 1.1-1.2 and the orthography appendix (Tables 16-17, pp.10-11): the work describes three level tones with minimal triplets (bál/bāl/bàl etc.), rising tones only in some numerals (Table 14: nǎn 'nine', lǔm 'ten'), and g…
new_statements.relation_note: Same statement as the existing_statements entry (Blench & Terna 2024, Sec. 2.3, p.4): the quote is verbatim in the on-disk text. The catalog record for Jaku / Labɨr has an empty rule, so there is nothing to contradict; this confirms the reading 'tone language, no stress statement'. Sec. 1.1 explicitly names the languoid: 'This is an introduction to the Jaku [jku] and glottocode [labi1245] language spoken in Bauchi State, Nigeria' and 'It is also known as Labir.' Minor quirk: Sec. 2.2 opens 'Gura has six vowels' (a template carry-over from Blench's Gura sketch), but Table 4 and the rest describe Jaku.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jaku is described as a three-level-tone language (High, Mid, Low; minimal triplets bál/bāl/bàl etc.), with no glide tones except rising tones heard in some numerals. The work says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence anywhere (whole main text a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits for stress/stressed/accent/prominence/pitch), so no stress placement can be read from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: rising tones occur in some numerals (Table 14: nǎn 'nine', lǔm 'ten') but not systematically in the lexicon; Sec. 2.2 notes no contrastive vowel length or nasalisation, long vowels heard in the dictionary data are unconfirmed.
new_statements.identity_note: The work is about Jaku proper (Labɨr/Labir), Sec. 1.1 giving the ISO code [jku] and glottocode [labi1245], Bauchi State, Nigeria; data collected with a Jaku working group in Jos, 2024. No dialect is singled out. Sec. 2.2 contains one stray 'Gura has six vowels' (template carry-over), but the vowel table and all examples are Jaku.
